title: Pair Pen
context: Grade 4, and this topic does the same job as the one before it by a quicker route while adding the idea the chapter actually wants. An adult sees multiplication facts being hunted. What is being built is the claim that a factor list is finite: it can be counted, because every factor is penned between one and the number and there are only so many whole numbers in that stretch. That claim is what the next topic needs, because multiples do the opposite and a child who has not watched one list shut cannot be shown the other one failing to.

writeup.why: Find the factors of a number by hunting the pairs that make it, and find out why that hunt always comes to an end.
writeup.look: A long pen with a post at each end, two dials underneath, and a ruled board between them where a pair is laid out as rows.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Pair Pen' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the first numbers tried against the first numbers there are to try, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each value is settled and the second fixed at the number itself, with the count of cards pinned in the pen beside them. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The pen runs across the top of the working area, 1086 by 156 at 64,202, with a solid post 24 wide standing at each of its ends: the left post carries one and the right post carries the chosen number, and both are drawn before any pair is hunted so the pen is visibly shut at both ends from the first frame. Pinned pairs lie inside it in order, each a linked card 96 by 104 carrying its two numbers joined by a drawn bar, so a pair moves as one piece and neither of its numbers can be pulled out alone. The two dials sit under the pen at 64,606 and 246,606, each 156 by 124, the left one driven upward from one. The ruled board stands between them and the pen, 700 by 340 at 450,246: laying a pair out draws exactly that many rows with exactly that many identical things in each, shut off from one another by drawn walls, never more than twenty in one visible group. A pair whose rows come to the number pins into the pen. A pair that overshoots is drawn running past the right post and is turned back with the overshoot left drawn; a pair that falls short leaves the gap drawn between its last row and the post. The run of first numbers is a ruled strip along the foot, 1086 by 76 at 64,646, with one place for every whole number from one upward: a place that failed keeps its own mark there rather than being dropped, and the pen refuses a pair while any lower place is still blank, lighting and naming the lowest blank one. The mirror light sits above the pen at 64,142 and comes on the moment a pinned pair is one already inside written the other way round, and the dials stop there. Count them closes both ends with a drawn bracket, shades the stretch between the posts, and reads the finished number of factors out. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a pair, a factor or a count is asked for, and on the third and fourth phases a word pad carrying the chapter's own words, factor, multiple, finite and infinite, so that a list can be described as well as counted. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number built by multiplying is green, anything standing in both lists at once is rose, whatever is left over and any trial that fails is vermilion, the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber, and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a trial that failed is told by the leftover standing outside its rows before it is told by a band, and a list that stops is told by the wall at each end of it before it is told by anything else. The two posts are furniture and never animate in. They are up before the first dial is touched, because a pen that acquires its ends after the hunting is over teaches that a list stops when the hunting does, which is the opposite of what this tool is for.
writeup.finish: The card shows the fullest pen the child built, both posts standing, every pinned pair in order and the finished count beside it.

phases.win: the pair pins into the pen and both numbers are read out as factors
phases.does: counts the rows, counts what is in each, and pins the pair
phases.goal: two numbers whose rows come to the number are a factor pair
phases.says: Count the rows, then count one row. What does that pair make?
phases.check: A tray holds 6 rows of 9 beads. Write that as a factor pair and name both of its factors.
phases.feels: two numbers, laid out as rows, and the rows come to exactly the number
phases.hands: Tip twenty-four counters onto the floor and ask for them to be put into equal rows, then into different equal rows, then again, until nobody can find another way. Each time, write the two numbers down as a pair: the number of rows and the number in each. Then lay six rows of nine beads out and ask for that pair and for the number it comes to, before anybody counts the whole lot one at a time.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many rows are on the board? Second rung, the phase's: how many are in one row, and what do the two of them come to? Third rung: the board is cut to a small pair and the child counts the rows and pins them. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the rows are what the eye lands on first and what the hands made, while the number in each row is something that has to be looked for a second time.
wrong.move: counts the rows and calls that the factor, leaving the number in each row unnamed.
wrong.screen: the ruled board is turned a quarter turn in front of the child and the same counters are read the other way round, so that the number in each row becomes the number of rows without a single counter moving. Both numbers are then lifted into a linked card with the bar drawn between them, and the card is pinned whole.

wrong.why: four rows of five looks orderly, and two counters at the end of a row read as part of the row rather than as a shortfall.
wrong.move: pins a pair that comes close, four rows of five for twenty-two, and lets the two spare counters sit on the end of a row.
wrong.screen: the pair is laid out on the ruled board as exactly four rows of exactly five, with the two spare counters standing outside the rows on the same surface at full strength. The rows are counted to twenty and the gap between the last row and the right post is drawn, so the pair is seen to fall short rather than to be nearly right. The child's pair stays where it was put.

phases.screen: a ruled board with one pair already laid out as rows and the pen empty
phases.soWhat: Two numbers that multiply to give the number are a factor pair of it, and both of them are factors.
phases.concept: Two numbers that make the number

phases.win: the mirror light comes on at the first repeat and the run stops there
phases.does: drives the first dial up one step at a time, pinning or failing each
phases.goal: the first number climbs from one, and the repeat is the stop signal
phases.says: Move the first dial up one at a time. Tell me when a pair comes back.
phases.check: Pair up the factors of 21 starting at 1. Which trials fail, and at which pair do you know you have finished?
phases.feels: the pairs come back to meet you, and that is the signal to stop
phases.hands: Pair up the factors of twenty-one on squared paper, starting the first number at one and moving it up a step at a time. Write a line for every value, including the ones that give nothing: one and twenty-one, then two fails, then three and seven, then four, five and six all fail, and then seven comes back with three. Ask what is new about that last pair, and stop the moment somebody says it is one they already have.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which is the lowest place on the run with nothing on it? Second rung, the phase's: could a value you skipped have made the number? Third rung: the run is cut to six places with a small number between the posts and the child walks it one place at a time. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: three trials in a row that give nothing make the next few look like a waste of time, and a child who is right about a number being unlikely is right often enough for the habit to survive.
wrong.move: drives the first dial straight past four, five and six because none of them looks at all likely.
wrong.screen: the pen refuses the pair and the lowest blank place on the run lights and is named. Each skipped value is then laid out on the ruled board in turn, with its rows drawn and its shortfall or its overshoot drawn beside them, and every one of those places keeps its mark along the run afterwards, so the run reads as unbroken rather than as tidy.

wrong.why: it arrived like every other pair, the rows came out right, and nothing about it announces that it has been here before.
wrong.move: pins the pair that came back as though it were a new one, so the same two numbers stand in the pen twice.
wrong.screen: the new card is drawn settling directly against its mirror rather than into a place of its own, and the mirror light fills. The pen is then counted out card by card with the count standing in the corner, and the count stops where it stopped before. Both cards stay drawn, one against the other.

phases.screen: the dials at one with the pen empty and every first number untried
phases.soWhat: Work the first number up from one, try every value in turn, and stop when a pair repeats one already pinned.
phases.concept: Going up in order, and knowing when the pairs repeat

phases.win: one and the number itself pin into the pen straight from the posts
phases.does: pins the outer pair from the posts alone, without touching the board
phases.goal: one and the number itself are factors of it before any work is done
phases.says: Name two of its factors before you do any work at all.
phases.check: Name the smallest factor and the greatest factor of 85, and say how you knew both without dividing anything.
phases.feels: two of them are already standing there before any work is done
phases.hands: Write any number your class likes on the board, fifty-seven will do, and ask for two of its factors before a single division is done. Take whatever is offered and test it. Then put one row of fifty-seven counters on the floor, and after that fifty-seven rows of one, and ask how many were left over either time. Finish by asking which two numbers are already known about every number on the board.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number is standing on the left post? Second rung, the phase's: which number is standing on the right post, and is it a factor too? Third rung: the pen is cut to a small number and the child pins the two outer cards straight from the posts. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: a factor that arrives without any dividing does not feel earned, and the interesting middle of the list looks like the answer the question was after.
wrong.move: leaves one and the number itself out of the pen, because neither of them took any work.
wrong.screen: both posts light and each is dropped through the board in front of the child: one row of fifty-seven, with nothing standing outside it, and fifty-seven rows of one, with nothing standing outside that either. The two cards pin, the pen is counted out with them in and then read again with them lifted to one side, and the two counts stand together.

wrong.why: the word factor sounds like a part of a thing, and a whole thing is not usually one of its own parts.
wrong.move: puts one into the pen but refuses the number itself, because a number cannot be a factor of itself.
wrong.screen: the number is laid on the board as a single row holding all of it, and the leftover shelf beside the board is drawn empty and read out as empty. The rule on the word pad is opened to the half that says less than OR EQUAL TO, with the equal half lit, and the right post is read out as the greatest factor there is. Nothing the child pinned is moved.

phases.screen: the pen empty with both end posts standing and no pair laid out yet
phases.soWhat: One is a factor of every number, and every number is a factor of itself.
phases.concept: The two factors every number has

phases.win: the pen reads out a finished count and nothing stands outside the two posts
phases.does: counts the pinned pairs and looks at where every one of them sits
phases.goal: every factor lies between one and the number, so the list can be counted
phases.says: Could this list go on for ever? Look at where the factors are standing.
phases.check: How many factors has 44, and how do you know there are no more of them?
phases.feels: you can count them, because there is nowhere else for a factor to be
phases.hands: Find every factor of forty-four together and pin them in a row on the board. Then rule a line from one to forty-four along the bottom of the page and mark every factor on it, so the whole list is sitting inside one stretch. Ask whether a factor could ever be found outside that stretch, and then ask the question the page keeps asking: not which numbers, but how many.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which two numbers are standing on the posts? Second rung, the phase's: could a factor stand outside them? Third rung: the pen is cut to a small number, the child fills it and then counts the cards out with a finger. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: factors and multiples are met within a day or two of each other and the list that ran off the edge of the frame is the one that is remembered, so for ever attaches itself to whichever of the two words comes up next.
wrong.move: says the factors could carry on for ever, the way the multiples on the track did.
wrong.screen: both posts light, the stretch between them is shaded, and the whole numbers inside it are counted out along the run. A number past the right post is then dropped onto the board and the rows it would need are drawn, running off the board without ever reaching the number; it is turned back at the post with the overshoot left drawn. The track from the topic before opens under the pen at the same time, leaving the frame with no end mark.

wrong.why: the numbers are what was hunted for and what is standing in the pen, so reading them out feels like the whole of the answer to any question about them.
wrong.move: answers how many factors by reading the list out, and never says a number at all.
wrong.screen: the question is read again with the words how many lit, and the cards in the pen are counted out one at a time with the count climbing in the corner as each is touched. The child's list stays exactly where it was written and the count is drawn underneath it, so the two answers stand together and neither replaces the other.

phases.screen: a full pen with both ends shut and the stretch between the posts shaded
phases.soWhat: Every factor lies between one and the number itself, so a factor list is finite and can be counted.
phases.concept: Why a factor list always ends

writeup.delight: The second phase, when the first dial reaches the pair that comes back. The new card travels along the pen looking for its place and settles directly against the pair already pinned, and the two are drawn as mirrors of each other: the bar between the numbers is the same bar, and the numbers read the same two either way round. The mirror light fills at that instant, the dials come to a stop on their own, and the whole run of first numbers along the foot lights from one up to where the finger got to, with every failed place still marked. Drive the dial on and the pen simply keeps handing back mirrors, one after another, and the count never moves.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase one pair is already laid out on the ruled board as rows, the pen standing empty with both posts up. On the second both dials are at one, the pen is empty and the run of first numbers is drawn beneath the board with every place on it still blank. On the third the board is bare and the pen is empty with the two posts standing and lit, the left post carrying one and the right post carrying the number itself. On the fourth the pen is full, the mirror light is on, and the stretch between the posts waits to be shaded. The running count at the top left holds the first numbers tried against the first numbers there are to try, with the count of cards pinned in the pen beside them, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the laid out pair, or the first dial, or the right hand post, or the last pinned pair, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the rows on the board come to. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number up to a hundred between the posts, both dials free, with the mirror light and the count control on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on reading a pair off rows of counters, working the pairs up in order, naming the two factors every number has, and counting a finished list.
voiceLines: Two posts go up first. One at this end, and the number itself at the other.
Count the rows, then count one row. What does that pair make?
Move the first dial up one at a time. Tell me when a pair comes back.
Name two of its factors before you do any work at all.
Could this list go on for ever? Look at where the factors are standing.
A new number between the posts. Start the first dial at one.
Free play. Any number between the posts, both dials free, the mirror light as you like.
Lay that pair out as rows and count them. What do they come to?
Shut at both ends, and every factor you found is standing inside.

observations.why: One and the number itself are factors of it whatever else turns out to be, so both ends are known in advance.
observations.soWhat: The list is shut at both ends from the start, and the hunting only fills the middle.
observations.observe: Both ends of the pen were standing before a single pair had been hunted.

observations.why: A factor cannot be greater than the number it divides, so there is nowhere outside the posts for one to stand.
observations.soWhat: A factor list is finite, which is why it can be counted.
observations.observe: Every pair that pinned had both of its numbers inside the two posts.

observations.why: Each pair has a smaller number and a bigger one, and once the first dial passes the middle it starts meeting pairs already pinned.
observations.soWhat: The first repeat is where the hunt finishes, and it arrives on its own.
observations.observe: The pairs began coming back the other way round instead of bringing anything new.

observations.why: A list names which numbers, and a count says how many, and a question asks for one of the two.
observations.soWhat: When a question asks how many, the count is part of the answer and not an afterthought.
observations.observe: Reading the pen out and counting the pen out were two different answers.

source_tool.description: A long pen runs across the stage with a post at each end. The left post is one and the right post is the number itself, and those two posts are put up before anything else, because every factor there is has to stand between them. Two dials below choose a pair of numbers, and a board between them lays that pair out as rows: the correct number of rows with the correct number in each, drawn on a ruled board so it can be counted. A pair whose rows come to the number is pinned into the pen; a pair that overshoots runs past the right post and is turned back, and a pair that falls short leaves a visible gap before it. The dials are driven up from one, and the pen will not take a pair while a smaller first number is still untried, so the run stays unbroken and every failure keeps its place. A mirror light comes on when a pair is the one already pinned written the other way round, which is where the list finishes. A count them control then shuts both ends and reads the pen out as a finished number of factors.
source_tool.art_direction: A fenced pen between two posts / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: trays of countable things, ruled rows on a board, a ladder of rungs with one trial to a rung, a pen with a wall at each end, a track of equal steps, cards that turn over, and two rings of cord that overlap.

Equal groups are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a row is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are in it, and the rows are kept apart by a drawn wall or a plain gap and never by colour alone.

Whatever is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the rows, on the same surface, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never crossed out, never tucked under a row and never left to be guessed from a gap. The leftover is the reason a trial failed, so it is the last thing any stage may hide.

A list of factors is drawn penned in between one and the number itself, with both ends of the run plainly stopped by a wall or a final post, so the list can be seen to end. A list of multiples is drawn running from the number away to the right, and the track carrying it leaves the frame with no end mark and no last step drawn, so the list can be seen not to end. The two never run the same way on one stage.

A run of trials is drawn unbroken. Every whole number from one up to the last one tried keeps its own rung or row, in order, with none left out, and a trial that fails is drawn and marked as a failure rather than dropped.
Where the digits of a number are added, every digit sits in its own cell, zeros included, and a cell holding a zero is drawn and counted in rather than left out of the line.
Nothing the child is asked to count one at a time comes to more than twenty things in one group. A larger quantity is a ruled array of identical tiles or a written numeral, never a loose heap.
A list is told apart by the wall or the open edge at its end first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a counter or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number that is built by multiplying is green, and anything standing in both lists at once is rose, and those three hold in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Whatever is left over, and any trial that fails, is vermilion; the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber; and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. All of that holds in greyscale, because a failed trial is told apart by the leftover drawn outside its row before it is told apart by colour, and a factor list is told apart from a list of multiples by the wall at each end of it before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Lay that pair out as rows and count them. What do they come to?
voice.onNext: A new number between the posts. Start the first dial at one.
voice.opening: Two posts go up first. One at this end, and the number itself at the other.
voice.onFinish: Shut at both ends, and every factor you found is standing inside.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any number between the posts, both dials free, the mirror light as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Two numbers that make the number
Going up in order, and knowing when the pairs repeat
The two factors every number has
Why a factor list always ends

placement.where: After a handful of counters has been laid out in equal rows on the floor and the pairs have been written down by hand. The tool is what puts up both end posts before the list is built, so the stopping can be watched rather than announced at the end.

answer_key.rule: A factor pair is two numbers that multiply to give the number, and both of them are factors of it. Work the first number up from one and try every value in turn. When a pair repeats one already found, written the other way round, every factor has been found. One is a factor of every number and every number is a factor of itself, so those two are known before any work starts. No factor is ever greater than the number it belongs to, so the whole list lies between one and the number, which is why it ends and can be counted. We say the factors of a number are finite.
answer_key.wrong: The pair is laid out again as rows on the ruled board and counted, so the child can see it come to more or less than the number, and the smallest untried first number is lit. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The rows are equal and nothing is left outside them, so the tray divides exactly.
4 times 17 is 68, so the two numbers multiply to give the number.
Any two numbers that multiply to give 68 are a pair of its factors.
items.answer: A factor pair of 68, so 4 and 17 are both factors of 68
items.question: A tray holds 4 rows of 17 seeds, which comes to 68 seeds. What does that make 4 and 17?
items.checkpoint: Two numbers that multiply to give the number are a factor pair of it.
items.misconception: Calling only the number of rows a factor and leaving out the number in each row.

steps: 1 and 21 pin at once, then 2 fails because no whole number of twos makes 21.
3 and 7 pin, and then 4, 5 and 6 all fail in turn and each failure keeps its place.
At 7 the pair is 7 and 3, which is 3 and 7 the other way round, so the list is finished.
items.answer: 1 and 21, then 3 and 7, so the factors are 1, 3, 7 and 21; the trials at 2, 4, 5 and 6 all fail
items.question: Pair up the factors of 21, working the first number up from 1, and say which trials fail.
items.checkpoint: Work the first number up from one, and stop when a pair repeats one already pinned.
items.misconception: Skipping the numbers that look unlikely, which leaves a gap the list cannot account for.

steps: 1 is a factor of every number, because one of anything divides it exactly.
Every number is a factor of itself, because it goes into itself once.
So 1 and 57 pin straight from the posts, and they are the smallest and the greatest of its factors.
items.question: Take the number 57. Can you name two of its factors before doing any dividing at all?
items.checkpoint: One is a factor of every number, and every number is its own greatest factor.
items.misconception: Thinking a number has to be tested before anything at all can be said about its factors.

steps: 1 and 34 pin from the posts, and 2 and 17 pin from the board.
Every other first number from 3 to 16 fails, and none of them can pin a pair.
No factor can be greater than 34, so the whole list is penned between the posts and can be counted.
items.answer: No. The factors are 1, 2, 17 and 34, and the list stops because every factor lies between 1 and 34
items.question: Could 34 have factors going on for ever? Find them all and say how you know the list stops.
items.checkpoint: The factors of a number are finite, which means you can count them.
items.misconception: Believing a bigger number could still turn up as a factor somewhere past the number itself.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: 5 rows of 13 counters come to 65 altogether. Write that as a factor pair of 65.
Write a factor pair of 22 that does not use 1.
Name the smallest factor of 58 and the greatest factor of 58.
items.final_answer: 1 is the smallest and 58 is the greatest

items.question: Pair up the factors of 46, working the first number up from 1, and say which trials fail.
items.final_answer: 1 and 46, then 2 and 23, so the factors are 1, 2, 23 and 46; every trial from 3 to 22 fails

items.question: A child pairing the factors of 27 writes 1 and 27, then jumps to 3 and 9. Which trial was skipped, and does it work?
items.final_answer: 2 was skipped, and it fails, because 27 divided by 2 leaves 1 over. The factors are 1, 3, 9 and 27

items.question: Is 1 a factor of 99? Is 99 a factor of 99?
items.final_answer: Yes to both, because 1 is a factor of every number and every number is a factor of itself

items.question: How many factors has 81, and how do you know there are no more?
items.final_answer: Five: 1, 3, 9, 27 and 81. The pairs repeat at 9 times 9, and no factor can be greater than 81, so the list stops

items.question: A stall has 78 pots and wants them in equal rows, with more than one row and more than one pot in a row. List every way.
items.final_answer: Six ways: 2 rows of 39, 3 rows of 26, 6 rows of 13, 13 rows of 6, 26 rows of 3 and 39 rows of 2

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: puts up one at the left and the number itself at the right before any work starts
chooses the two numbers of a pair, the first driven up from one
draws the pair as rows on a ruled board so it can be counted
pins a pair whose rows come to the number into the pen
refuses a pair while a smaller first number is still untried
comes on when a pair is one already pinned, the other way round
shuts both ends and reads the pen out as a finished count of factors

teaching_notes: Put both end posts up before the first pair is hunted, and say why they are there: every factor has to stand between them, and that single fact is what makes the list end. Otherwise finite arrives as a word to be remembered rather than a thing that was watched happening. Drive the first dial up one step at a time and refuse to let anybody jump, even when the class is certain a number cannot work, because the certainty is the thing being tested and it is wrong often enough to matter. Make a point of a number where several trials in a row fail, so that a run of failures stops looking like a mistake. The mirror light is the moment to slow right down: ask what is new about the pair that just came up, and get the answer that it is one they already have, written back to front. Finish on the count. A class that can say how many factors a number has, and why there are no more, is ready for the next topic, where the same question about multiples has no answer at all.
generation_prompt: Build a factor pairing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A long horizontal pen runs across the stage with a solid post at each end, the left post carrying one and the right post carrying the chosen number, both drawn before any work begins so the pen is visibly closed at both ends. Two dials below select a pair of numbers. A ruled board between the dials and the pen lays the chosen pair out as rows, drawing exactly that many rows with exactly that many identical things in each, separated by drawn walls rather than by colour, never more than twenty in a visible group. A pair whose rows come to the number pins into the pen as a linked card. A pair that overshoots runs past the right post and is turned back with the overshoot drawn; a pair that falls short leaves the gap drawn before the post. The first dial is driven upward from one and the pen refuses a pair while any smaller first number is untried, lighting and naming the untried one. A failed first number keeps its own marked place along the run rather than being dropped. A mirror light comes on the moment a pinned pair is one already in the pen written the other way round, and the dials stop there. A count them control then closes both ends with a bracket, shades the stretch between the posts, and reads out the finished number of factors. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put up the two posts first, one and the number itself. Move the first dial up from one, a step at a time. Lay each pair out as rows and count them. Pin the pairs that make the number. Stop when a pair comes back the other way round, then count what is in the pen.
